about: Fluid Mechanics 1 (MECH40002) is a 5-ECTS core module in Year 1 of Imperial's Mechanical Engineering MEng, taught in the Autumn and Summer terms (2026–27 programme specification). A third-party copy of the module description (UC Education Abroad, last reviewed 2023–24) says it builds the foundations in four stages: the mathematical description of fluids, fluid statics, fluid dynamics analysed with control volumes, and application to internal flows. Imperial's full topic list was not available to us, so the eight topics here expand those four stages into a standard first-year course, in the same order. We could not confirm the module's assessment breakdown; check the department's module page.
topics: Fundamental concepts: fluids, the continuum and fluid properties
Fluid statics: pressure, the hydrostatic equation and manometry
Fluid statics: forces on submerged surfaces, buoyancy and stability
Fluids in motion: describing flow and conservation of mass
Fluids in motion: Bernoulli's equation and flow measurement
Fluids in motion: the control-volume momentum equation
Internal flows: laminar and turbulent pipe flow
Internal flows: head losses and pipe systems

notes.h: What a fluid is and the properties that describe it
notes.body:
Fluid mechanics starts with a precise idea of what a fluid is and which properties control its behaviour.

Definition
- A fluid is a substance that deforms continuously under a shear stress, however small. A solid under a small shear stress deforms by a fixed amount and stops; a fluid keeps flowing for as long as the stress acts.
- A fluid at rest therefore carries no shear stress: only pressure (a normal stress).
- Liquids keep a fixed volume and form a free surface; gases expand to fill their container.

The continuum hypothesis
We treat the fluid as continuous, so that density, velocity and pressure are smooth functions of position and time. This works when the length scales of the problem are much larger than the spacing (or mean free path) of the molecules, which is true for almost all engineering flows. It breaks down in very rarefied gases.

Key properties (typical values at about 20 °C)
- Density ρ (kg/m³): water ≈ 1000 (998), air ≈ 1.2. Specific weight γ = ρg (N/m³). Relative density (specific gravity) SG = ρ/ρ_water; mercury SG ≈ 13.6.
- Dynamic viscosity μ (Pa s): the resistance to shear. For a Newtonian fluid, τ = μ du/dy. Water μ ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa s; air ≈ 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa s.
- Kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ (m²/s): water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶; air ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁵.
- Viscosity of liquids falls with temperature; viscosity of gases rises with temperature.
- Bulk modulus K = −V dp/dV: water ≈ 2.2 GPa, so liquids are usually treated as incompressible. Gases are much more compressible, but low-speed gas flows (Mach number below about 0.3) can also be treated as incompressible.
- Surface tension σ (N/m): water–air ≈ 0.073 N/m. Capillary rise in a tube of diameter d: h = 4σ cos θ/(ρgd). For water in a clean 1 mm glass tube (θ ≈ 0), h ≈ 30 mm.
- Vapour pressure: if local pressure falls below it, the liquid boils (cavitation), which damages pumps and propellers.

The no-slip condition
A viscous fluid in contact with a solid surface has the same velocity as that surface. This creates velocity gradients near walls, which is where viscous shear stresses act.

Worked example: viscous drag on a sliding plate
A plate of area 0.5 m² slides at 2 m/s on an oil film 1 mm thick (μ = 0.1 Pa s). Assuming a linear velocity profile (Couette flow):
- τ = μU/h = 0.1 × 2/0.001 = 200 Pa.
- Force F = τA = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N.

Non-Newtonian fluids
Fluids whose shear stress is not proportional to shear rate (e.g. paint, blood, toothpaste) are non-Newtonian. This module deals with Newtonian fluids.

Exam tips: always convert mm to m before using τ = μU/h; quote units for viscosity carefully (Pa s for μ, m²/s for ν); state the continuum and no-slip assumptions when you use them.

notes.h: Pressure in a fluid at rest and how we measure it
notes.body:
In a fluid at rest there is no shear stress, so the only stress is pressure. Fluid statics asks how pressure varies through the fluid and what forces it produces.

Pressure at a point
- Pressure is a normal compressive stress, p = dF/dA (Pa = N/m²).
- In a static fluid, pressure at a point is the same in all directions (Pascal's law), which follows from equilibrium of a small wedge of fluid as it shrinks to a point.

The hydrostatic equation
Vertical equilibrium of a small fluid element with z measured upwards gives
dp/dz = −ρg
- For a liquid of constant density: p = p₀ + ρgh, where h is depth below a surface at pressure p₀.
- Pressure depends only on depth, not on the shape of the container (the "hydrostatic paradox").
- Points at the same level in the same continuous fluid at rest have the same pressure.
- Example: at 10 m depth in water, the gauge pressure is ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98.1 kPa, almost one atmosphere.

Absolute and gauge pressure
- Absolute pressure is measured from a perfect vacuum. Gauge pressure is measured relative to local atmospheric pressure: p_gauge = p_abs − p_atm.
- Standard atmospheric pressure is 101.325 kPa.
- A mercury barometer measures atmospheric pressure: p_atm = ρ_Hg g h, giving h ≈ 760 mm.

Manometers
Manometers use columns of liquid to measure pressure differences. The method is always the same: start at one point, add ρgh going down and subtract ρgh going up through each fluid, and set the result equal to the pressure at the end point.
- Piezometer: a simple open tube; p = ρgh.
- U-tube manometer: uses a heavier gauge fluid (often mercury) to measure larger pressures.
- Differential manometer: measures the pressure difference between two points in a pipe.

Worked example: differential manometer
Water flows in a pipe; a mercury U-tube connected between two tappings at the same level shows a mercury level difference of 0.2 m. The water fills the tubes above the mercury. Walking through the fluids:
- p₁ + ρ_w g(a + h) − ρ_Hg g h − ρ_w g a = p₂ (where a is the water depth above the upper mercury level on the low-pressure side).
- The a terms cancel, giving p₁ − p₂ = (ρ_Hg − ρ_w)gh = (13 600 − 1000) × 9.81 × 0.2 ≈ 24.7 kPa.
Forgetting the water above the mercury would give 26.7 kPa, an error of about 8%.

Variation in a gas
For a gas, ρ changes with p, so dp/dz = −ρg must be combined with the ideal gas law. For small height changes (a few metres) the change in gas pressure is negligible, which is why pressure in a gas-filled tank is usually taken as uniform.

Exam tips: mark every interface on a sketch, write one equation from end to end, and state whether answers are gauge or absolute.

notes.h: Forces on submerged surfaces, buoyancy and floating stability
notes.body:
Pressure acting over a surface produces a resultant force. Designing dams, gates, tanks, ships and submarines needs both its size and its line of action.

Plane surfaces
For a plane surface of area A, at any inclination, wholly submerged in a liquid with its centroid at depth h_c:
- Resultant force F = ρ g h_c A = (pressure at the centroid) × area. It acts normal to the surface.
- The force acts at the centre of pressure, which is below the centroid for any non-horizontal surface because pressure increases with depth (on a horizontal surface the pressure is uniform and the two coincide).
- Measured along the plane of the surface from the free-surface line: y_cp = y_c + I_c/(y_c A), where I_c is the second moment of area of the surface about a horizontal axis through its centroid.
- For a vertical rectangle of height d with its top at the surface, y_cp = 2d/3 below the surface.

Worked example
A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge at the water surface.
- h_c = 1.5 m, A = 6 m², so F = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.5 × 6 = 88.3 kN.
- I_c = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴, so y_cp = 1.5 + 4.5/(1.5 × 6) = 2.0 m below the surface (two-thirds of the depth).
If the same gate were lowered so that its top was 2 m below the surface, h_c = 3.5 m, F = 206 kN and y_cp = 3.5 + 4.5/21 ≈ 3.71 m: the centre of pressure moves towards the centroid as the gate gets deeper.

Curved surfaces
- Horizontal component: equal to the force on the vertical projection of the surface, acting through its centre of pressure.
- Vertical component: equal to the weight of fluid directly above the surface (real or imaginary) up to the free surface.
- The resultant combines the two; for a circular surface it passes through the centre of curvature.

Buoyancy (Archimedes' principle)
A body immersed in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces, acting through the centroid of the displaced volume (the centre of buoyancy, B). A floating body displaces its own weight of fluid.

Stability of floating bodies
- A fully submerged body is stable only if its centre of gravity G lies below B.
- A floating body can be stable even with G above B, because B moves sideways when the body heels.
- Metacentric height GM = BM − BG (or KB + BM − KG, measured from the keel K). Stable if GM > 0.
- BM = I/V, where I is the second moment of the waterplane area about the axis of heel and V the submerged volume.

Example: a rectangular barge 20 m long, 6 m wide, floating at a draft of 1.5 m with G 2.0 m above the keel.
- BM = (L B³/12)/(L B d) = B²/(12d) = 36/18 = 2.0 m.
- KB = d/2 = 0.75 m, so KM = 2.75 m and GM = 2.75 − 2.0 = 0.75 m: stable.

Exam tips: the centre of pressure is always below the centroid for an inclined or vertical surface; for curved surfaces calculate components separately; use I/V for BM, with I about the axis of rolling (the long axis for a ship rolling sideways).

notes.h: Describing fluid motion and conserving mass
notes.body:
Before applying conservation laws to moving fluids we need a vocabulary for describing flow and the idea of a control volume.

Lagrangian and Eulerian descriptions
- Lagrangian: follow individual fluid particles and record their properties as they move (like tracking one car).
- Eulerian: describe the flow field at fixed points in space as functions of position and time, e.g. V(x, y, z, t) (like a speed camera at a fixed location). Fluid mechanics mostly uses the Eulerian view.
- The acceleration of a particle in an Eulerian field is the material (substantial) derivative: DV/Dt = ∂V/∂t + (V·∇)V. The first term is the local acceleration; the second is the convective acceleration.
- Steady flow (∂/∂t = 0 everywhere) can still have accelerating particles: fluid speeds up through a nozzle because of convective acceleration.

Visualising flow
- Streamline: a line everywhere tangent to the velocity at an instant. No flow crosses a streamline.
- Pathline: the actual path of one particle over time.
- Streakline: the line formed by all particles that have passed through a fixed point (what you see with continuous dye or smoke injection).
- In steady flow streamlines, pathlines and streaklines coincide.
- A streamtube is a bundle of streamlines; fluid cannot cross its walls.

Classifying flows
- Steady or unsteady; uniform or non-uniform (changing with position).
- One-, two- or three-dimensional.
- Laminar or turbulent; viscous or inviscid (idealisation); compressible or incompressible.

System and control volume
- A system is a fixed mass of fluid; mechanics laws (Newton's second law, conservation of mass) are written for systems.
- A control volume (CV) is a region of space chosen by the analyst, through whose boundary (the control surface) fluid can flow. The Reynolds transport theorem converts system laws into CV form. Choosing a sensible CV is the key skill in this module.

Conservation of mass for a control volume
Rate of increase of mass inside the CV = mass flow rate in − mass flow rate out.
For steady flow: Σ ṁ_in = Σ ṁ_out, where ṁ = ρ V A (V the mean velocity normal to the area).
For incompressible flow: volume flow rate Q = V A is constant along a pipe, so A₁V₁ = A₂V₂.

Worked example
Water flows at 2 m/s in a 100 mm diameter pipe that reduces to 50 mm.
- Q = A₁V₁ = (π × 0.1²/4) × 2 = 0.0157 m³/s.
- V₂ = V₁ (D₁/D₂)² = 2 × 4 = 8 m/s.
Velocity scales with the inverse square of the diameter, not the inverse of the diameter.

Mean velocity
In real pipe flow velocity varies across the section. The mean velocity is defined by V = Q/A = (1/A)∫u dA, and continuity is applied using mean velocities.

Exam tips: draw and label the control volume; mark inflows and outflows; use mass flow (ρVA) when density changes, as in gas flows.

Bernoulli's equation is an energy balance along a streamline for an idealised flow. It is the most used (and misused) equation in introductory fluid mechanics.

Statement
For steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline, with no shaft work or heat transfer:
p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant
or, dividing by ρg, in terms of head (metres of fluid):
p/(ρg) + V²/(2g) + z = H (total head).
- p/(ρg): pressure head; V²/(2g): velocity head; z: elevation head.
- In pressure form: static pressure p, dynamic pressure ½ρV², and stagnation (total) pressure p₀ = p + ½ρV² (when z changes are negligible).
- It can be derived by applying Newton's second law to a fluid particle along a streamline (Euler's equation) and integrating.

Assumptions to state every time
Steady; inviscid (no friction losses); incompressible; along a single streamline (or across streamlines if the flow is irrotational); no pumps, turbines or heat transfer between the two points. Real pipe flows violate the inviscid assumption, and losses are added later through head-loss terms.

Applications
- Free jet from a tank (Torricelli): V = √(2gh). From 5 m depth, V ≈ 9.9 m/s.
- Pitot tube: measures stagnation pressure where the flow is brought to rest. With a static tapping, V = √[2(p₀ − p)/ρ]. In air (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) a difference of 500 Pa gives V ≈ 28.9 m/s. A Pitot–static tube combines both tappings and is used on aircraft for airspeed.
- Venturi meter: a smooth contraction to a throat. Combining Bernoulli and continuity between the inlet (1) and throat (2):
  V₂ = √{2(p₁ − p₂)/[ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²)]}, Q = C_d A₂ V₂.
  C_d (discharge coefficient) is typically about 0.95–0.99 for a venturi, allowing for small losses.
- Orifice plates are cheaper but have much larger losses and lower discharge coefficients (around 0.6).

Worked example: venturi meter
A venturi has inlet diameter 100 mm and throat 50 mm in a water line; the measured pressure difference is 15 kPa.
- A₂/A₁ = 0.25, so 1 − 0.25² = 0.9375.
- V₂ = √(2 × 15 000/(1000 × 0.9375)) = √32 ≈ 5.66 m/s.
- Ideal Q = A₂V₂ = (π × 0.05²/4) × 5.66 ≈ 0.0111 m³/s (11.1 L/s). With C_d = 0.98 this becomes about 10.9 L/s.
Leaving out the (A₂/A₁)² term would give 10.8 L/s ideal, an error of about 3%.

Hydraulic and energy grade lines
- Energy grade line (EGL): the total head H plotted along a pipe.
- Hydraulic grade line (HGL): p/(ρg) + z, which lies a velocity head below the EGL.
- With no losses the EGL is horizontal. Where the HGL falls below the pipe, the pressure is below atmospheric (risk of cavitation or air ingress).

Exam tips: choose points 1 and 2 where you know most quantities (free surfaces have p = p_atm and often V ≈ 0); always combine Bernoulli with continuity; check that pressures stay above vapour pressure.

notes.h: The momentum equation for a control volume
notes.body:
To find forces exerted by flowing fluids (on pipe bends, nozzles, vanes, jets, engines) we apply Newton's second law to a control volume.

Linear momentum equation (steady flow)
ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in
- ΣF is the vector sum of all external forces on the fluid in the CV: pressure forces on the control surface, forces from solid walls (the unknown we usually want), and body forces (weight).
- ṁ = ρVA at each inlet and outlet; V is a vector, so apply the equation separately in x and y.
- With one inlet and one outlet: ΣF = ṁ(V_out − V_in).
- The force exerted by the fluid on the solid is equal and opposite to the force of the solid on the fluid (Newton's third law).

Method
1. Draw a CV that cuts the flow where velocities and pressures are known, and cuts through any solid whose reaction you want.
2. Choose axes. Mark all forces on the fluid: p₁A₁ pushing into the CV at the inlet, p₂A₂ pushing into the CV at the outlet, the unknown reaction R from the solid, and weight if vertical.
3. Write momentum in each direction with correct signs for the velocity components.
4. Use gauge pressures if atmospheric pressure acts all round the outside.

Jet striking a flat plate
A jet of area A and speed V hits a stationary flat plate normal to it and spreads out sideways.
- All the x-momentum is destroyed, so the force on the plate is F = ṁV = ρAV².
- Example: 50 mm jet at 20 m/s: A = 1.96 × 10⁻³ m², ṁ = 39.3 kg/s, F ≈ 785 N.
- If the plate moves away from the jet at speed u, the relative velocity is V − u and the mass flow reaching the plate is ρA(V − u), so F = ρA(V − u)². At u = 8 m/s: F ≈ 283 N.
- A vane that turns the jet back through 180° roughly doubles the force (ideal value 2ρAV²).

Pipe bends
A horizontal 90° reducing bend carries water at Q = 0.1 m³/s from a 200 mm inlet (p₁ = 200 kPa gauge, flow in +x) to a 150 mm outlet (flow in +y). Neglecting losses:
- V₁ = 3.18 m/s, V₂ = 5.66 m/s; Bernoulli gives p₂ ≈ 189 kPa.
- x: p₁A₁ + R_x = ṁ(0 − V₁), so R_x = −318 − 6283 ≈ −6600 N.
- y: −p₂A₂ + R_y = ṁV₂, so R_y = 566 + 3341 ≈ 3907 N.
- The fluid pushes the bend with about 6.60 kN in +x and 3.91 kN in −y: a resultant of about 7.7 kN that the pipe supports or thrust blocks must resist.
Note that the pressure terms dominate; forgetting them is the most common error.

Other applications
Rocket and jet engine thrust, forces on nozzles (which tend to be pushed off the hose), and reaction forces on sprinklers. Angular momentum (torque = rate of change of angular momentum) extends the idea to turbomachines.

Exam tips: always draw the CV and a force diagram on the fluid; include pressure forces at every cut; say clearly whether your answer is the force on the fluid or on the solid.

notes.h: Laminar and turbulent flow in pipes
notes.body:
Internal flows (in pipes and ducts) are where viscosity matters most. The first question is always whether the flow is laminar or turbulent.

Reynolds' experiment and the Reynolds number
Osborne Reynolds (1883) injected dye into water flowing in a glass tube. At low speeds the dye stayed as a smooth thread (laminar); at higher speeds it broke up and mixed across the pipe (turbulent).
The controlling group is the Reynolds number:
Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν
the ratio of inertial to viscous forces.
- Pipe flow is normally laminar for Re below about 2000–2300.
- It is usually fully turbulent above about 4000; between these values it is transitional, and the exact value depends on inlet conditions and disturbances.
- Example: water (ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s) at 2 m/s in a 100 mm pipe: Re = 2 × 0.1/10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁵, firmly turbulent. Most water and air pipe flows in engineering are turbulent; slow, viscous oil flows are often laminar.

Developing and fully developed flow
- Near the inlet a boundary layer grows on the wall until it fills the pipe; after this entrance length the velocity profile stops changing and the flow is fully developed.
- Laminar entrance length is roughly L_e ≈ 0.06 Re D; for turbulent flow it is much shorter relative to Re (often 10–60 diameters).

Fully developed laminar flow (Hagen–Poiseuille)
A force balance on a cylinder of fluid of radius r and length L gives the shear stress τ = (Δp/L)(r/2), varying linearly from zero on the axis to a maximum at the wall. With τ = −μ du/dr this integrates to a parabolic profile:
- u(r) = u_max(1 − r²/R²), with u_max = 2V (twice the mean velocity).
- Pressure drop: Δp = 32μLV/D² = 128μLQ/(πD⁴).
- In Darcy form, f = 64/Re.
Example: oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa s) at a mean speed of 0.5 m/s in a 20 mm tube: Re = 90 (laminar), f = 0.711, and over 10 m Δp = 32 × 0.1 × 10 × 0.5/0.02² = 40 kPa.
The strong D⁴ dependence means halving the diameter at fixed flow rate multiplies the pressure drop by 16.

Turbulent pipe flow
- Turbulence produces random velocity fluctuations that mix momentum across the pipe, giving a much flatter mean profile (u_max ≈ 1.2V) and much steeper gradients at the wall, so wall friction is higher than for laminar flow at the same Re.
- No exact analytical solution exists; friction is found from experiments and empirical correlations (for example the Blasius formula f ≈ 0.316 Re⁻⁰·²⁵ for smooth pipes at moderate Re, up to about 10⁵), summarised in the Moody chart.
- A thin viscous sublayer remains next to the wall; surface roughness matters once roughness elements poke through it.

Exam tips: always compute Re first and say which regime applies; use the mean velocity V = Q/A in Re; remember f = 64/Re only for laminar flow.

notes.h: Head losses and the design of pipe systems
notes.body:
Real pipe flows lose mechanical energy to friction. Engineers need to predict these losses to size pipes and choose pumps.

Energy equation with losses
Between two points 1 and 2 on a pipeline (in head form):
p₁/(ρg) + V₁²/(2g) + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/(ρg) + V₂²/(2g) + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L
h_L is the total head loss: major (friction) losses along straight pipe plus minor losses at fittings.

Major losses: the Darcy–Weisbach equation
h_f = f (L/D) V²/(2g)
- f is the Darcy friction factor (dimensionless). (Be careful: some texts use the Fanning factor, which is one quarter of the Darcy value.)
- Laminar flow: f = 64/Re.
- Turbulent flow: f depends on Re and relative roughness ε/D. The Colebrook equation, 1/√f = −2.0 log₁₀[(ε/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re√f)], is implicit; the explicit Haaland approximation is 1/√f ≈ −1.8 log₁₀[((ε/D)/3.7)¹·¹¹ + 6.9/Re].
- The Moody chart plots these. At very high Re in rough pipes the curves flatten: f depends only on ε/D (fully rough regime).
- Example: commercial steel (ε ≈ 0.045 mm), D = 100 mm, Re = 2 × 10⁵: Colebrook gives f ≈ 0.0186 (Haaland ≈ 0.0184).
- Example: f = 0.02, L = 50 m, D = 0.1 m, V = 2 m/s gives h_f = 0.02 × 500 × 4/19.62 ≈ 2.04 m (a pressure drop of about 20 kPa in water).

Minor losses
h_m = K V²/(2g) for each fitting. Typical values: sharp-edged pipe entrance K ≈ 0.5; exit into a large reservoir K = 1.0 (the whole velocity head is lost); standard 90° elbow K of order 0.3–1.5 depending on type; open gate valve small, partly closed valves much larger.

Pumps
- Hydraulic power delivered to the fluid: P = ρ g Q h_pump.
- Shaft power required = ρ g Q h_pump/η, where η is the pump efficiency.

Worked example: gravity-fed pipeline
A reservoir's surface is 20 m above the outlet of a 100 m long, 100 mm diameter pipe that discharges as a free jet to atmosphere. Take f = 0.02 and an entrance loss K = 0.5.
- Energy from reservoir surface to the jet: 20 = (1 + 0.5 + 0.02 × 100/0.1) V²/(2g) = 21.5 V²/(2g).
- V = √(2 × 9.81 × 20/21.5) ≈ 4.27 m/s; Q ≈ 0.0336 m³/s.
- Check: Re ≈ 4.3 × 10⁵, turbulent, consistent with f ≈ 0.02.
Without losses the jet would leave at √(2g × 20) ≈ 19.8 m/s, so friction dominates this system.

Pipes in series and parallel
- In series: the same Q flows through each pipe and the head losses add.
- In parallel: the head loss across each branch is the same and the flows add.

Solving pipe problems
- Type 1: find h_L given Q and D (direct).
- Type 2: find Q given h_L (iterate: guess f, find V, update Re and f).
- Type 3: find D given Q and h_L (iterate).

Exam tips: list every loss term before writing the energy equation; remember the exit velocity head (or the K = 1 exit loss into a tank); check Re after finding V to confirm your friction factor.

ν = μ/ρ, in m²/s. Water ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s; air ≈ 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m²/s at about 20 °C.

cards.f: Gauge pressure at 10 m depth in water

cards.b: p₁ − p₂ = (ρ_Hg − ρ_w) g h, where h is the difference in mercury levels.
Pressure at a given depth depends only on depth and density, not on the shape or volume of the container.

cards.f: Mercury barometer height at standard atmosphere
cards.b: About 760 mm, from p_atm = ρ_Hg g h with ρ_Hg ≈ 13 600 kg/m³.

cards.f: Resultant force on a submerged plane surface
cards.b: F = ρ g h_c A: pressure at the centroid × area, acting normal to the surface.

cards.f: Centre of pressure on a plane surface
cards.b: y_cp = y_c + I_c/(y_c A), measured along the plane from the free-surface line; below the centroid for any non-horizontal surface (they coincide on a horizontal one).

cards.f: Vertical rectangle with top edge at the surface: centre of pressure
cards.b: At two-thirds of the height below the surface.

cards.f: Vertical force on a curved submerged surface
cards.b: Equal to the weight of fluid (real or imaginary) vertically above the surface up to the free surface.
The buoyant force equals the weight of fluid displaced and acts through the centroid of the displaced volume (centre of buoyancy).
GM = BM − BG, with BM = I/V (waterplane second moment / displaced volume). Floating body is stable if GM > 0.

cards.f: Stability of a fully submerged body
cards.b: Stable only if the centre of gravity is below the centre of buoyancy, because B does not move as the body tilts.
Describing the flow by fields at fixed points in space, e.g. V(x, y, z, t), rather than following individual particles.
DV/Dt = ∂V/∂t + (V·∇)V: local acceleration plus convective acceleration of a fluid particle.
A line everywhere tangent to the instantaneous velocity; no flow crosses it.

cards.f: When do streamlines, pathlines and streaklines coincide?
cards.b: In steady flow.
A chosen region of space through whose surface fluid may flow; conservation laws are applied to it using inflows and outflows.

cards.f: Continuity for steady incompressible pipe flow
cards.b: Q = A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, so V₂ = V₁(D₁/D₂)² in circular pipes.
ṁ = ρVA (kg/s), using the mean velocity normal to the area.
p + ½ρV² + ρgz = constant along a streamline for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow with no work or heat transfer.
p₀ = p + ½ρV²: the pressure reached when the flow is brought to rest without losses (z changes neglected).
Efflux speed from a tank V = √(2gh), h the depth of the outlet below the free surface (losses ignored).
V = √[2(p₀ − p)/ρ], using the difference between stagnation and static pressures.
Q = C_d A₂ √{2Δp/[ρ(1 − (A₂/A₁)²)]}, A₂ the throat area.
p/(ρg) + z along a pipe; lies one velocity head V²/2g below the energy grade line.
Steady, inviscid, incompressible flow along a streamline, with no shaft work or heat transfer between the points.
ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in, applied as a vector (separately in x and y) to the fluid in a control volume.

cards.f: Force on a stationary flat plate from a normal jet
cards.b: F = ṁV = ρAV²: all incoming momentum normal to the plate is destroyed.

cards.f: Force on a single flat plate moving away at speed u
cards.b: F = ρA(V − u)²: both the relative velocity and the mass flow reaching the plate are reduced.

cards.f: Forces to include on a control volume
cards.b: Pressure forces at each inlet and outlet, reaction forces from solid boundaries, and body forces such as weight.

cards.f: Force of fluid on a pipe bend
cards.b: Equal and opposite to the reaction R found from the momentum equation for the fluid in the bend.

cards.f: Ideal force from a jet turned through 180°
cards.b: 2ρAV² for a stationary vane: twice the force on a flat plate.
Re = ρVD/μ = VD/ν: ratio of inertial to viscous forces. V is the mean velocity, D the diameter.
Laminar below about Re = 2000–2300; turbulent above about 4000; transitional between.
Parabolic: u = u_max(1 − r²/R²), with u_max = 2 × mean velocity.
Δp = 32μLV/D² = 128μLQ/(πD⁴) for fully developed laminar pipe flow.

cards.f: Shear stress distribution in fully developed pipe flow
cards.b: τ = (Δp/L)(r/2): zero at the centre, maximum at the wall (laminar or turbulent).

cards.f: Why turbulent wall friction is higher
cards.b: Turbulent mixing flattens the mean profile, so the velocity gradient (and shear stress) at the wall is much larger.
h_f = f (L/D) V²/(2g), with f the Darcy friction factor.
h_m = K V²/(2g) for a fitting, bend, valve, entrance or exit.

cards.f: Loss coefficient at a sharp-edged entrance and at an exit into a reservoir
cards.b: About 0.5 at a sharp entrance; 1.0 at the exit into a large reservoir (all velocity head lost).
At high Re in a rough pipe, the friction factor depends only on relative roughness ε/D, not on Re.
P = ρ g Q h_pump/η, where h_pump is the head added and η the pump efficiency.
Series: same Q, head losses add. Parallel: same head loss across each branch, flows add.
Darcy f = 4 × Fanning f. Check which one a chart or formula uses.
1/√f = −2.0 log₁₀[(ε/D)/3.7 + 2.51/(Re√f)]: implicit correlation for turbulent f; basis of the Moody chart.

questions.q: A plate of area 0.5 m² slides at 2 m/s over a 1 mm oil film of viscosity 0.1 Pa s. Assuming a linear velocity profile, what force is needed to keep it moving?
questions.why: τ = μU/h = 0.1 × 2/0.001 = 200 Pa, and F = τA = 200 × 0.5 = 100 N. 200 N quotes the shear stress (in Pa) as if it were the force, forgetting to multiply by the area. 0.1 N leaves the film thickness in millimetres (h = 1 instead of 0.001 m). 400 N divides the stress by the area instead of multiplying.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a fluid from a solid?
options: A fluid deforms continuously under any shear stress, however small
A fluid cannot carry any normal stress
questions.why: The defining property is continuous deformation under shear. 'Cannot carry normal stress' is wrong because fluids carry pressure, which is a normal stress. 'Zero viscosity' describes an idealised inviscid fluid, not real fluids. 'Always incompressible' is wrong because gases are highly compressible; incompressibility is only a modelling assumption for liquids and low-speed gas flows.

questions.q: Explain the continuum hypothesis and the no-slip condition, and give one situation in which each might break down or need care.
markScheme: Continuum: fluid treated as continuous; properties defined at a point as smooth fields
Valid when length scales ≫ molecular mean free path / spacing; breaks down in rarefied gas (e.g. very high altitude, micro-scale gas flows)
No-slip: fluid velocity at a wall equals wall velocity
Consequence: velocity gradients and shear stress near walls (boundary layers); care needed in rarefied flow or with superhydrophobic surfaces
questions.modelAnswer: The continuum hypothesis treats a fluid as continuous matter, so that density, pressure and velocity can be defined at every point as smooth fields, even though the fluid is really made of molecules. It is valid when the length scales of interest are much larger than the molecular mean free path; it breaks down in very rarefied gases, such as flows at very high altitude or in micro-scale gas channels. The no-slip condition says that a viscous fluid in contact with a solid has the same velocity as the solid. It is why velocity gradients, shear stresses and boundary layers form near walls. It too can fail in rarefied gases, where some slip occurs at the wall.

questions.q: What is the gauge pressure 10 m below the free surface of a water tank open to the atmosphere?
questions.why: p_gauge = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 10 = 98 100 Pa = 98.1 kPa. 199.4 kPa adds atmospheric pressure (101.3 kPa), giving the absolute pressure rather than the gauge pressure. 9.81 kPa uses a depth of 1 m. 10.0 kPa leaves out g (ρh = 1000 × 10 = 10 000).

questions.q: A mercury U-tube manometer (ρ_Hg = 13 600 kg/m³) connects two tappings at the same level on a water pipe. The tubes above the mercury are full of water and the mercury levels differ by 0.2 m. What is the pressure difference between the tappings?
questions.why: p₁ − p₂ = (ρ_Hg − ρ_w)gh = 12 600 × 9.81 × 0.2 ≈ 24.7 kPa. 26.7 kPa uses ρ_Hg alone, ignoring the column of water that sits on top of the mercury. 1.96 kPa uses the density of water only, as if the gauge fluid were water. 2.52 kPa uses (ρ_Hg − ρ_w)h but leaves out g.

questions.q: Derive the hydrostatic equation dp/dz = −ρg by considering the equilibrium of a small element of fluid, and hence show that pressure increases linearly with depth in a liquid.
markScheme: Sketch: element of area dA, height dz, z upward
Forces: p dA on bottom, (p + dp/dz dz) dA on top, weight ρg dA dz
Vertical equilibrium gives dp/dz = −ρg
Integrate with constant ρ: p = p₀ + ρgh (h depth below surface)
questions.modelAnswer: Consider a small vertical cylinder of fluid of cross-sectional area dA and height dz, with z measured upwards. The pressure on its bottom face is p, giving an upward force p dA; on the top face it is p + (dp/dz)dz, giving a downward force [p + (dp/dz)dz]dA. Its weight is ρg dA dz downwards. There are no shear stresses in a fluid at rest, so the side forces are horizontal and cancel. Vertical equilibrium gives p dA − [p + (dp/dz)dz]dA − ρg dA dz = 0, so dp/dz = −ρg. For a liquid of constant density, integrating from the free surface (pressure p₀) down to depth h gives p = p₀ + ρgh, so pressure rises linearly with depth.

questions.q: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high has its top edge at the free surface of water. What is the resultant hydrostatic force on it?
questions.why: F = ρ g h_c A = 1000 × 9.81 × 1.5 × 6 = 88.3 kN. 176.6 kN uses the pressure at the bottom of the gate (depth 3 m) over the whole area instead of the pressure at the centroid. 44.1 kN leaves out the 2 m width (uses an area of 3 m²). 9.0 kN leaves out g (1000 × 1.5 × 6 = 9000).

questions.q: A rectangular barge 20 m long and 6 m wide floats at a draft of 1.5 m. Its centre of gravity is 2.0 m above the keel. What is its metacentric height for rolling about the long axis?
questions.why: BM = B²/(12d) = 36/18 = 2.0 m, KB = 0.75 m, so GM = KB + BM − KG = 0.75 + 2.0 − 2.0 = 0.75 m (stable). 2.0 m is BM alone, not GM. 2.75 m is KM, which forgets to subtract the height of G. 0 m leaves out KB, taking GM = BM − KG.

questions.q: A vertical rectangular gate 2 m wide and 3 m high is submerged with its top edge 2 m below the water surface. Calculate the resultant force and the depth of the centre of pressure, and comment on how the centre of pressure moves as the gate is lowered further.
markScheme: y_cp = 3.5 + 4.5/(3.5 × 6) ≈ 3.71 m below the surface
As depth increases, I_c/(y_c A) shrinks, so the centre of pressure approaches the centroid
questions.modelAnswer: The centroid is at h_c = 2 + 1.5 = 3.5 m below the surface and A = 2 × 3 = 6 m², so F = ρ g h_c A = 1000 × 9.81 × 3.5 × 6 ≈ 206 kN. The second moment of area about a horizontal axis through the centroid is I_c = 2 × 3³/12 = 4.5 m⁴. For a vertical surface y_cp = y_c + I_c/(y_c A) = 3.5 + 4.5/21 ≈ 3.71 m below the surface, 0.21 m below the centroid. As the gate is lowered, y_c increases so the correction I_c/(y_c A) shrinks: the pressure becomes more uniform across the gate and the centre of pressure moves towards the centroid.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m/s in a 100 mm pipe that reduces to 50 mm diameter. What is the velocity in the smaller pipe?
questions.why: A₁V₁ = A₂V₂, so V₂ = 2 × (100/50)² = 8 m/s. 4 m/s scales with the diameter ratio instead of its square (area ratio). 0.5 m/s inverts the area ratio, as if the fluid slowed down in the smaller pipe. 2 m/s assumes velocity is conserved, which would violate conservation of mass.

questions.q: Water flows steadily through a converging nozzle. Which statement about the acceleration of a fluid particle is correct?
options: It is non-zero because of convective acceleration, even though the local acceleration is zero
It is zero because the flow is steady
It is zero because the fluid is incompressible
It is non-zero because the local acceleration ∂V/∂t is non-zero
questions.why: In steady flow ∂V/∂t = 0, but particles move into regions of higher velocity, so the convective term (V·∇)V is non-zero. 'Zero because steady' confuses the local derivative at a fixed point with the total acceleration following a particle. 'Zero because incompressible' is wrong: incompressibility fixes the volume flow rate, which is exactly why the velocity must rise as the area falls. 'Local acceleration non-zero' contradicts the definition of steady flow.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a streamline, a pathline and a streakline, and state when they are the same.
markScheme: Streamline: tangent to instantaneous velocity field (snapshot)
Pathline: trajectory of a single particle over time
Streakline: locus of all particles that have passed through a fixed point (dye/smoke)
In steady flow all three coincide
questions.modelAnswer: A streamline is drawn at one instant so that it is everywhere tangent to the velocity vector; no fluid crosses it. A pathline is the actual trajectory traced by one particular fluid particle over time, like a long-exposure photograph of a single tracer. A streakline joins all the particles that have passed through a particular fixed point, which is what you see when dye or smoke is injected continuously at one location. In unsteady flow these three lines differ, but in steady flow the velocity field does not change, so particles follow the streamlines and all three coincide.

questions.q: A venturi meter with inlet diameter 100 mm and throat diameter 50 mm carries water. The pressure difference between inlet and throat is 15 kPa. What is the ideal flow rate?
questions.why: V₂ = √[2 × 15 000/(1000 × (1 − 0.25²))] = 5.66 m/s and Q = A₂V₂ = 0.001963 × 5.66 ≈ 0.0111 m³/s. 0.0108 m³/s ignores the inlet velocity, using V₂ = √(2Δp/ρ). 0.0444 m³/s multiplies the throat velocity by the inlet area instead of the throat area. 0.00785 m³/s leaves out the factor 2 inside the square root.

questions.q: A Pitot–static tube in an airflow (ρ = 1.2 kg/m³) reads a difference of 500 Pa between stagnation and static pressure. What is the air speed?
questions.why: V = √(2Δp/ρ) = √(2 × 500/1.2) ≈ 28.9 m/s. 20.4 m/s leaves out the factor 2 (√(500/1.2)). 1.0 m/s uses the density of water instead of air. 833 m/s forgets to take the square root (2 × 500/1.2 = 833).

questions.q: Water drains from a large open tank through a small hole in its side, 5 m below the free surface. State the assumptions needed to apply Bernoulli's equation and find the jet speed. Explain why the measured flow rate through a sharp-edged hole is less than A√(2gh).
markScheme: Steady (large tank: surface falls slowly), inviscid, incompressible, along a streamline from surface to jet
Surface and jet both at atmospheric pressure; surface velocity ≈ 0
Actual flow lower due to vena contracta (jet contracts) and small friction losses
Expressed by discharge coefficient C_d ≈ 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice
questions.modelAnswer: Take a streamline from the free surface (point 1) to the jet just outside the hole (point 2). Assume quasi-steady flow (the tank is large, so its level falls slowly and V₁ ≈ 0), inviscid and incompressible flow, and that both points are at atmospheric pressure. Bernoulli gives ρg × 5 = ½ρV₂², so V₂ = √(2 × 9.81 × 5) ≈ 9.9 m/s. In practice the jet from a sharp-edged hole contracts to a smaller area (the vena contracta) a short distance downstream, and there are small friction losses that reduce the velocity slightly. Both effects are combined in a discharge coefficient, Q = C_d A√(2gh), with C_d about 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice.

questions.q: A 50 mm diameter water jet travelling at 20 m/s strikes a stationary flat plate at right angles and spreads out along it. What force does it exert on the plate?
questions.why: F = ρAV² = 1000 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 20² ≈ 785 N. 393 N is ½ρAV², the dynamic pressure times area, which confuses Bernoulli with the momentum equation. 39.3 N is the mass flow rate ρAV in kg/s, without multiplying by the velocity change. 1571 N is 2ρAV², which applies to a vane turning the jet back through 180°, not to a flat plate.

questions.q: The same jet (50 mm, 20 m/s) strikes a single flat plate that is moving directly away from the nozzle at 8 m/s. What force does it exert on the plate?
questions.why: Relative to the plate the jet arrives at 12 m/s and the mass reaching the plate per second is ρA × 12, so F = ρA(V − u)² = 1000 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 144 ≈ 283 N. 785 N ignores the plate's motion. 471 N is ρAV(V − u), which uses the full jet mass flow; that is correct for a series of vanes (as on a Pelton wheel) that intercepts all the jet, but not for a single receding plate. 660 N uses ρA(V² − u²), which subtracts squared speeds instead of squaring the relative speed.

questions.q: Water flows through a horizontal 90° reducing bend at 0.1 m³/s. The inlet (diameter 200 mm, flow in +x) has gauge pressure 200 kPa; the outlet (diameter 150 mm) discharges in +y. Neglecting losses, find the x and y components of the force the water exerts on the bend.
markScheme: V₁ = 3.18 m/s, V₂ = 5.66 m/s from continuity
p₂ = p₁ + ½ρ(V₁² − V₂²) ≈ 189 kPa from Bernoulli
x-momentum: p₁A₁ + R_x = −ṁV₁ gives R_x ≈ −6.60 kN
y-momentum: −p₂A₂ + R_y = ṁV₂ gives R_y ≈ +3.91 kN
Force on bend = −R: 6.60 kN in +x and 3.91 kN in −y (resultant ≈ 7.7 kN)
questions.modelAnswer: A₁ = 0.0314 m² and A₂ = 0.0177 m², so V₁ = 0.1/0.0314 = 3.18 m/s and V₂ = 0.1/0.0177 = 5.66 m/s; ṁ = 100 kg/s. Bernoulli (horizontal, no losses): p₂ = 200 000 + 500(3.18² − 5.66²) ≈ 189 kPa gauge. Take a control volume around the water in the bend, with R the force from the bend on the water. x: p₁A₁ + R_x = ṁ(0 − V₁), so R_x = −100 × 3.18 − 200 000 × 0.0314 = −318 − 6283 ≈ −6600 N. y: the outlet pressure acts on the CV in −y, so −p₂A₂ + R_y = ṁV₂ and R_y = 566 + 3341 ≈ 3907 N. The force of the water on the bend is the reverse: about 6.60 kN in the +x direction and 3.91 kN in the −y direction, a resultant of about 7.7 kN.

questions.q: Oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa s) flows at a mean speed of 0.5 m/s in a 20 mm diameter tube. What is the pressure drop over 10 m of fully developed flow?
questions.why: Re = 900 × 0.5 × 0.02/0.1 = 90, so the flow is laminar and Δp = 32μLV/D² = 32 × 0.1 × 10 × 0.5/0.02² = 40 kPa. 160 kPa uses the radius (0.01 m) in place of the diameter in D². 80 kPa uses the centre-line velocity (2V = 1 m/s) instead of the mean velocity. 5.8 kPa uses the turbulent Blasius friction factor 0.316 Re⁻⁰·²⁵ at Re = 90, where only f = 64/Re applies.

questions.q: In fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe, what is the ratio of the centre-line velocity to the mean velocity?
questions.why: The parabolic Hagen–Poiseuille profile gives u_max = 2V. 1.5 is the ratio for laminar flow between two parallel plates, not in a pipe. 1.0 would be uniform (plug) flow with no viscous effects. About 1.2 is typical of turbulent pipe flow, whose mean profile is much flatter.

questions.q: Starting from a force balance on a cylinder of fluid in fully developed laminar pipe flow, show that the velocity profile is parabolic and that the centre-line velocity is twice the mean velocity.
markScheme: Force balance on cylinder radius r, length L: Δp πr² = τ 2πrL, so τ = Δp r/(2L)
Newtonian: τ = −μ du/dr
Integrate with u(R) = 0 (no slip): u = Δp(R² − r²)/(4μL), parabolic
u_max at r = 0: ΔpR²/(4μL)
Mean V = Q/A = (1/πR²)∫u 2πr dr = ΔpR²/(8μL) = u_max/2
questions.modelAnswer: Take a cylinder of fluid of radius r and length L on the pipe axis. In fully developed flow there is no change of momentum, so the net pressure force Δp πr² balances the wall-direction shear force τ × 2πrL on its curved surface: τ = Δp r/(2L). For a Newtonian fluid τ = −μ du/dr (u decreases outwards), so du/dr = −Δp r/(2μL). Integrating and applying no slip, u(R) = 0, gives u = Δp(R² − r²)/(4μL), a parabola with maximum u_max = ΔpR²/(4μL) on the axis. The flow rate is Q = ∫₀ᴿ u 2πr dr = πΔpR⁴/(8μL), so the mean velocity is V = Q/(πR²) = ΔpR²/(8μL) = u_max/2.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m/s through 50 m of 100 mm diameter pipe with a Darcy friction factor of 0.02. What is the friction head loss?
questions.why: h_f = f(L/D)V²/(2g) = 0.02 × 500 × 4/19.62 ≈ 2.04 m. 1.02 m uses V instead of V². 4.08 m leaves out the 2 in 2g. 0.204 m uses L instead of L/D (it forgets to divide by the 0.1 m diameter).

questions.q: In the fully rough turbulent regime of the Moody chart, the Darcy friction factor depends on which quantity?
options: Neither: it is a constant 0.02 for all pipes
questions.why: When roughness elements protrude well through the viscous sublayer, the loss is dominated by form drag on them and f becomes independent of Re. 'Reynolds number only' describes laminar flow (f = 64/Re) or hydraulically smooth pipes. 'Both' describes the transitional turbulent region covered by the Colebrook curves before they flatten. A constant 0.02 is just a common rough estimate for water pipes, not a law.

questions.q: A pump delivers water at 0.05 m³/s from a large reservoir through a 100 mm pipe of total length 100 m (Darcy f = 0.02, entrance K = 0.5). The pipe discharges as a free jet to atmosphere at a point 20 m below the reservoir surface. Find the head the pump must add and the shaft power needed if its efficiency is 75%.
markScheme: Energy equation surface to jet: 20 + h_p = (1 + 0.5 + fL/D) V²/(2g), with fL/D = 20
Hydraulic power ρgQh_p = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 × 24.4 ≈ 12.0 kW
Shaft power = 12.0/0.75 ≈ 16.0 kW
questions.modelAnswer: The pipe area is π × 0.1²/4 = 0.007854 m², so V = 0.05/0.007854 = 6.37 m/s and V²/(2g) = 2.07 m. Apply the energy equation from the reservoir surface (p = p_atm, V ≈ 0, z = 20 m above the outlet) to the free jet at the outlet (p = p_atm, z = 0, velocity V): 20 + h_p = V²/(2g) + 0.5V²/(2g) + f(L/D)V²/(2g) = (1 + 0.5 + 20) × 2.07 ≈ 44.4 m. So h_p ≈ 24.4 m. The hydraulic power is ρgQh_p = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 × 24.4 ≈ 12.0 kW, and the shaft power is 12.0/0.75 ≈ 16.0 kW. Without the pump, gravity alone would drive only about 0.034 m³/s through this pipe.

questions.q:
Water flows from a large reservoir through a horizontal pipe of length 100 m and diameter 100 mm, discharging as a free jet to atmosphere at a point 20 m below the reservoir's free surface. Take the Darcy friction factor as 0.02, the entrance loss coefficient as 0.5, ν = 1.0 × 10⁻⁶ m²/s and g = 9.81 m/s².
(a) State the energy equation between the reservoir surface and the jet, listing each loss term. [4]
(b) Find the velocity in the pipe and the flow rate. [5]
(c) Check the flow regime and comment on whether f = 0.02 is reasonable for a commercial steel pipe (ε ≈ 0.045 mm). [4]
(d) A pump is added to raise the flow rate to 0.05 m³/s. Find the pump head and the shaft power at 75% efficiency. [5]
(e) Sketch the energy and hydraulic grade lines for part (b). [2]
markScheme: (a) z₁ = V²/(2g) + K V²/(2g) + f(L/D)V²/(2g), with p = p_atm and V ≈ 0 at the surface
(c) Re = VD/ν ≈ 4.3 × 10⁵: turbulent
(c) ε/D = 0.00045; Colebrook/Moody gives f ≈ 0.0175, so 0.02 is a reasonable slightly conservative estimate
(d) Shaft power = ρgQh_p/η ≈ 16.0 kW
(e) EGL starts at reservoir level, drops 0.5V²/2g at entrance then falls linearly; HGL is V²/2g below EGL, reaching the pipe at the outlet
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Take point 1 on the reservoir surface (p = p_atm, V ≈ 0, z = 20 m above the outlet) and point 2 in the jet at the outlet (p = p_atm, velocity V, z = 0). The losses are the entrance loss 0.5V²/(2g) and the pipe friction loss f(L/D)V²/(2g). The energy equation is 20 = V²/(2g) + 0.5V²/(2g) + f(L/D)V²/(2g), where the first term on the right is the kinetic energy carried away by the jet.

(b) f(L/D) = 0.02 × 100/0.1 = 20, so 20 = 21.5V²/(2g). Then V² = 2 × 9.81 × 20/21.5 = 18.25, V ≈ 4.27 m/s. The area is π × 0.1²/4 = 0.007854 m², so Q ≈ 0.0336 m³/s (33.6 L/s).

(c) Re = VD/ν = 4.27 × 0.1/10⁻⁶ ≈ 4.3 × 10⁵, so the flow is fully turbulent. With ε/D = 0.045/100 = 0.00045, the Colebrook equation (or the Moody chart) gives f ≈ 0.0175 at this Re. The assumed 0.02 is therefore a reasonable, slightly conservative estimate; repeating the calculation with f = 0.0175 gives V ≈ 4.5 m/s, about 6% more flow.

(d) For Q = 0.05 m³/s, V = 0.05/0.007854 = 6.37 m/s and V²/(2g) = 2.07 m. The energy equation becomes 20 + h_p = 21.5 × 2.07 ≈ 44.4 m, so h_p ≈ 24.4 m. The hydraulic power is ρgQh_p = 1000 × 9.81 × 0.05 × 24.4 ≈ 12.0 kW and the shaft power is 12.0/0.75 ≈ 16.0 kW.

(e) The energy grade line starts at the reservoir surface level, drops by the entrance loss (0.5 × 0.93 ≈ 0.47 m) at the pipe inlet, then falls linearly by about 18.6 m along the pipe, ending one velocity head (≈ 0.93 m) above the outlet. The hydraulic grade line runs parallel to it, one velocity head lower, and meets the pipe centre-line at the outlet where the pressure is atmospheric.

questions.q:
A horizontal 90° reducing bend carries water at 0.1 m³/s. At the inlet the diameter is 200 mm, the flow is in the +x direction and the gauge pressure is 200 kPa. At the outlet the diameter is 150 mm and the flow leaves in the +y direction. Atmospheric pressure acts on the outside of the bend.
(a) Explain why gauge pressures can be used in the analysis. [2]
(b) Find the velocities at inlet and outlet and, neglecting losses, the outlet pressure. [5]
(c) Draw a suitable control volume and write the steady momentum equation in the x and y directions. [5]
(d) Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force exerted by the water on the bend. [6]
(e) State how your answer would change if the real bend had a head loss of 0.5 m. [2]
markScheme: (a) Atmospheric pressure acts all round a closed control surface and gives zero net force, so only gauge pressure produces a net force
(b) V₁ = 3.18 m/s, V₂ = 5.66 m/s from Q = AV
(b) p₂ = p₁ + ½ρ(V₁² − V₂²) ≈ 189 kPa gauge
(c) CV around the fluid in the bend; forces p₁A₁ (+x), p₂A₂ (−y), R_x, R_y on the fluid
(c) x: p₁A₁ + R_x = ṁ(0 − V₁); y: −p₂A₂ + R_y = ṁ(V₂ − 0)
(d) R_x ≈ −6.60 kN, R_y ≈ +3.91 kN on the fluid
(d) Force on bend ≈ 7.67 kN at about 30.6° below the +x axis (6.60 kN in +x, 3.91 kN in −y)
(e) Outlet pressure lower by ρg × 0.5 ≈ 4.9 kPa, so p₂A₂ and the y component fall slightly (by about 87 N)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A uniform atmospheric pressure acting over the whole of a closed surface produces zero net force. Since atmospheric pressure acts on the outside of the bend, subtracting it everywhere leaves gauge pressures as the only pressures that produce a net force on the control volume.

(b) A₁ = π × 0.2²/4 = 0.03142 m² and A₂ = π × 0.15²/4 = 0.01767 m². V₁ = 0.1/0.03142 = 3.18 m/s and V₂ = 0.1/0.01767 = 5.66 m/s. With no losses and no height change, p₂ = p₁ + ½ρ(V₁² − V₂²) = 200 000 + 500(10.13 − 32.02) ≈ 189 100 Pa = 189 kPa gauge.

(c) Take a control volume enclosing the water inside the bend, cutting the flow at the inlet and outlet. The forces on this water are: p₁A₁ acting in +x at the inlet (pushing into the CV); p₂A₂ acting in −y at the outlet (also pushing into the CV); and the unknown force from the bend walls, (R_x, R_y). Weight acts vertically, out of the horizontal plane, and does not enter. The mass flow is ṁ = ρQ = 100 kg/s.
x: p₁A₁ + R_x = ṁ(V_out,x − V_in,x) = ṁ(0 − V₁)
y: −p₂A₂ + R_y = ṁ(V_out,y − V_in,y) = ṁ(V₂ − 0)

(d) p₁A₁ = 200 000 × 0.03142 = 6283 N and ṁV₁ = 318 N, so R_x = −318 − 6283 = −6601 N. p₂A₂ = 189 100 × 0.01767 = 3341 N and ṁV₂ = 566 N, so R_y = 566 + 3341 = 3907 N. The force of the water on the bend is equal and opposite: F_x = +6601 N, F_y = −3907 N. Its magnitude is √(6601² + 3907²) ≈ 7670 N (7.67 kN), acting at tan⁻¹(3907/6601) ≈ 30.6° below the +x axis, i.e. the bend is pushed outwards and downstream of its inlet direction. The pipe supports or a thrust block must provide this force.

(e) A head loss of 0.5 m lowers the outlet pressure by ρg × 0.5 = 4.9 kPa, to about 184 kPa. That reduces p₂A₂ by about 87 N, so F_y falls in magnitude to about 3.82 kN while F_x is unchanged; the overall force drops only slightly.
